The '''Neugebauer equations''' are a set of equations used to model [[color printing]] systems, developed by [[Hans E. J. Neugebauer]].<ref name=original>{{cite journal |first=H. E. J. |last=Neugebauer |title=Die theoretischen Grundlagen des Mehrfarbenbuchdrucks |trans-title=The theoretical foundations of multicolor printing |journal=Zeitschrift für wissenschaftliche Photographie Photophysik und Photochemie |volume=36 |issue=4 |date=1937 |pages=73–89}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Color Technology for Electronic Imaging Devices |first=Henry R. |last=Kang |publisher=SPIE Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-8194-2108-1 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/colortechnologyf00kang}}</ref> They were intended to predict the color produced by a combination of [[halftone]]s printed in [[CMYK|cyan, magenta, and yellow inks]].

The equations estimate the [[reflectance]] (in [[CIE XYZ]] coordinates or as a function of wavelength) as a function of the reflectance of the 8 possible combinations of CMY inks (or the 16 combinations of CMYK inks), weighted by the area they take up on the paper. In wavelength form:<ref name=original />
: <math>R(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{16} w_i R_i(\lambda),</math>
where ''R<sub>i</sub>''(''λ'') is the reflectance of ink combination ''i'', and ''w<sub>i</sub>'' is the relative proportions of the 16 colors in a uniformly colored patch. The weights are dependent on the halftone pattern and possibly subject to various forms of [[dot gain]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=Raja |last=Balasubramanian |title=A spectral Neugebauer model for dot-on-dot printers |journal=Proc. SPIE |volume=2413 |date=1995 |doi=10.1117/12.207594 |s2cid=109388624 |url=http://chester.xerox.com/~raja/papers/EI95.pdf}}</ref>

Light can interact with the paper and ink in more complex ways. The [[Yule-Nielsen effect|Yule–Nielsen]] correction takes into account light entering through blank regions and re-emerging through ink:<ref>{{cite journal |first1=J. A. C. |last1=Yule |first2=W. J. |last2=Neilsen |date=1951 |title=The Penetration of light into Paper and its Effect on Halftone Reproduction |volume=1951 |journal=TAGA Proceedings |pages=65–76}}</ref>
: <math>R(\lambda) = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{16} w_i R_i(\lambda)^\frac{1}{n} \right)^n.</math>
The factor ''n'' would be 2 for a perfectly diffusing [[Lambertian reflectance|Lambertian]] paper substrate, but can be adjusted based on empirical measurements. Further considerations of the optics, such as multiple internal reflections, can be added at the price of additional complexity.

In order to achieve a desired reflectance, these equations have to be inverted to produce the actual dot areas or digital values sent to the printer, a nontrivial operation that may have multiple solutions.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Marc F. |last=Mahy |editor-first1=Giordano B. |editor-first2=Reiner |editor-last1=Beretta |editor-last2=Eschbach |date=1998 |title=Insight into the solutions of the Neugebauer equations |journal=Electronic Imaging: SPIE/IS&T International Technical Group Newsletter |series=Color Imaging: Device-Independent Color, Color Hardcopy, and Graphic Arts III |volume=3300 |issue=Jan 1999 |pages=7, 11  |doi=10.1117/12.298265 |bibcode=1998SPIE.3300...76M |s2cid=5328092 |url=http://www.inventoland.net/pdf/Reports/ei_newsletter99ocr.pdf}}</ref>
